census:g1:grid-19.basis: Payoff imitation coupled with conformity on lattices is documented: Szolnoki & Perc 2015 (conformists smooth interfaces, change cooperation level) and Lin et al. 2020 (combined payoff/conformity rule in the spatial PD is always absorbed into a frozen full-C or full-D state). Noise-triggered avalanches on a near-frozen Nowak-May lattice are documented by Lim, Chen & Jayaprakash 2002.
census:g1:grid-19.difference: No source couples rare stochastic majority adoption applied to every cell with deterministic imitate-best (Moore+self, strict PD). Szolnoki & Perc use a fixed conformist fraction with Fermi updating on a k=4 lattice; Lin et al. report absorption, not a sustained near-frozen state with bursts; Lim et al.'s perturbations come from stochastic updating, not majority flips. The combined signature (99%-frozen game kept active by majority-triggered bursts, dominance pulled to ~96%) is not described.
census:g1:grid-19.citation_problems: No fabrication. The BioSystems paper is cited without authors (Newth & Cornforth 2009) and its quoted detail is unverified. Szolnoki & Chen 2018 is a coevolutionary model in which the learning method spreads, not 'payoff imitation combined with conformity' in the card's sense. None of the cited sources covers the coupling.

census:novelty:grid-4.basis: Vilone et al. 2014 study this coupling (unconditional imitation, or voter copying with probability q) in the PD and find that adding social imitation drives finite systems to consensus (frozen all-C or all-D) for most parameters; at small q the approach is slow and UI-dominated. Vilone et al. 2012 show the same UI+voter mix turns UI-frozen domain patterns on 2D lattices into global consensus. Consensus as the absorbing state of finite voter-type dynamics is stated explicitly. Remaining differences (random networks in 2014, a coordination game in 2012, T=1.4/P=epsilon vs T=1.3/P=0, sequential synchronous application here) do not change the absorbing-state outcome.
census:novelty:grid-4.citation_problems: None fabricated. Stage 3 calls Vilone et al. 2014 'the same pair of rules' without noting that it uses Erdos-Renyi and scale-free networks rather than a lattice; the 2012 lattice paper (not cited by Stage 3) closes that gap.

qd:004.basis: Lin et al. 2020: a spatial PD with a rule combining payoff-driven and conformity-driven updating is always absorbed into a frozen full-C or full-D state. Szolnoki & Chen 2018 study competition between payoff and conformity learning across the snowdrift quadrant of a square lattice.
qd:004.difference: The documented absorption is for the PD. For the snowdrift game, imitate-best alone keeps both types (sub-program never collapses; Roca et al. 2009 show UI fosters cooperation at T=1.5), and no source shows that adding majority adoption collapses a snowdrift lattice to one type. Szolnoki & Chen's learning method is a coevolving trait, not a per-step majority rule applied to all cells.
qd:004.citation_problems: Hauert & Doebeli 2004 is cited for the lattice behaviour of this imitate-best snowdrift model, but their lattice results use the replicator rule; under unconditional imitation the snowdrift lattice favours cooperation at T=1.5 (Roca et al. 2009), so the 'cooperation can die out' framing does not transfer. Stage 3 cited no source at all for the majority-rule coupling (it said it relied on general knowledge).

qd:005.basis: Vilone et al. 2014 (PD, random networks) and 2012 (coordination game, 2D lattices) show that mixing unconditional imitation with voter copying drives the system toward consensus, with voter acting as interface noise. Roca et al. 2009 document snowdrift under unconditional imitation on k=8 lattices (game alone).
qd:005.difference: Same coupling, but no source pairs voter copying with imitate-best in the snowdrift game, whose anti-coordination payoffs oppose coarsening. The measured partial ordering (94% one type, falling activity) is consistent with Vilone's consensus drift but is not reported for this game; Stage 3 itself says it found no snowdrift-plus-voter paper.
qd:005.citation_problems: None fabricated. Hauert & Doebeli's quoted lattice result does not apply to imitate-best dynamics (replicator rule; see Roca et al. 2009).

qd:012.basis: Vainstein & Arenzon 2014, Sicardi et al. 2009 and Vainstein, Silva & Arenzon 2007 study synchronous imitate-the-best PD and snowdrift games with random mobility on square lattices; mobility changes cooperation levels and fast diffusion approaches the well-mixed limit.
qd:012.difference: Their mobility is jumps into empty sites on diluted von Neumann lattices (none at full occupancy); here neighbours swap contents on a fully occupied Moore+self lattice every step. The combined signature (activity raised above the swap-only level, intermediate domain count) is not reported.
qd:012.citation_problems: None fabricated. Stage 3 did not note that all cited mobility studies use dilution and moves into empty sites, unlike swaps on a full lattice.

qd:013.basis: Payoff imitation plus conformity on lattices is documented: Szolnoki & Perc 2015 (conformists add surface tension and smooth interfaces; full conformity gives neutral drift), Cui & Wu 2013 (conformity plus payoff-biased transmission can reach high or full cooperation), Lin et al. 2020 (combined rule always absorbed).
qd:013.difference: Documented couplings use a fixed conformist fraction with Fermi updating on a k=4 lattice, or a combined stochastic rule that always ends absorbed (Lin et al. 2020). None reports a persistent ~25/75 mixture sustained by per-step majority adoption where imitate-best alone nearly fixes one strategy; the measured persistence differs from Lin et al.'s absorption.
qd:013.citation_problems: CSF 2018 is cited by PII only; it is Yang, Huang, Dai & Yang, 'The effects of attribute persistence on cooperation in evolutionary games'. Stage 3 did not open full texts (it says so), so it missed that the documented couplings end absorbed rather than in persistent coexistence.

qd:015.basis: Coevolutionary PD with imitate-best and rewiring is documented (Zimmermann, Eguiluz & San Miguel 2004; Zimmermann & Eguiluz 2005). Rewiring of opposite-strategy links competing with strategy updating, giving like-strategy communities, is studied by Chen et al. 2010 (Chin. Phys. B 19:050205, found by reviewer). Synchronous updating in a coevolving PD produces oscillations of cooperation and linkage (Biely, Dragosits & Thurner 2007, Physica D 228:40, found by reviewer).
qd:015.difference: Zimmermann-Eguiluz and Lee et al. rewire only cooperator-defector links, initiated by the cooperator, toward random nodes; Biely et al. use rational, non-imitative updates; Chen et al. report community splitting, not oscillation. No source shows strategy-homophilic rewiring by both types amplifying node-state oscillation of synchronous imitate-best at T=1.9.
qd:015.citation_problems: J. Complex Networks paper given without authors (Lee, Malik & Mucha). Stage 3 left open whether 'type' is the strategy; in the simulator (census/sim.py, _N_GAME and _N_REWIRE) it is the same variable, so the rewiring is strategy-homophilic for both cooperators and defectors, which none of the cited models use. The 'great oscillations at temptations 1.7-1.95' quote is unattributed.

qd:016.basis: Lin et al. 2020 (spatial PD, combined payoff/conformity rule, always absorbed into full-C or full-D); Szolnoki & Perc 2015 (conformity pulls payoff-driven players into compact domains); Szolnoki & Chen 2018 (payoff vs conformity learning in the snowdrift quadrant).
qd:016.difference: Absorption under payoff plus conformity is documented only for the PD; snowdrift imitate-best alone coexists (sub-program largest domain 0.83), and no source reports majority adoption collapsing a snowdrift lattice to one type, nor the transient spectral peak.
qd:016.citation_problems: Hauert & Doebeli misapplied to imitate-best dynamics. Lin et al. 2020 is accurately quoted but is a PD result; Stage 3 acknowledged the game difference only as a 'minor twist'.

qd:023.basis: Grujic et al. 2010: imitate-the-best on a Moore lattice gives cooperation either 0 or close to 1 depending on the initial condition. Vilone et al. 2014: adding voter copying to unconditional imitation in the PD drives finite systems to a frozen all-C or all-D consensus for most parameters, slowly when q is small. Fixation in an absorbing state for this coupling is therefore stated in near-equivalent systems. Differences: networks rather than a lattice in Vilone; experiment payoffs and no self-interaction in Grujic.
qd:023.citation_problems: arXiv 0901.0355 and the textbook page are cited as bare URLs with no stated claim; 0901.0355 is mainly about best-response dynamics. Stage 3 cited no source for the voter coupling or for fixation under it.

qd:031.basis: Payoff imitation plus conformity in the spatial PD is documented to end absorbed in a frozen full-C or full-D state (Lin et al. 2020); conformity removes rough interfaces (Szolnoki & Perc 2015); imitate-best alone gives near 0 or near 1 cooperation (Grujic et al. 2010).
qd:031.difference: A stochastic threshold-6 majority flip applied to all cells with deterministic imitate-best (Moore+self, S=-0.5) is not modelled anywhere found; the specific combination effect (clearing the residual minority while generating bursty sporadic flips in a near-uniform lattice) is not described.
qd:031.citation_problems: Grujic et al. 2010 simulated a 13x13 lattice with the experiment's payoff matrix, not S=-0.5, so it supports the strict-PD claim only by analogy. Stage 3's reading of the 'cyclic' rule as a majority rule for two types is correct.

qd:039.basis: Saif & Gade 2009 (arXiv 0910.0955) add one-way C->D noise to Nowak-May imitate-best (Moore+self): an active coexistence phase below a critical p and an absorbing all-D phase above. Szabo, Vukov & Szolnoki 2005 map noise-driven mixed-to-all-D transitions on 2D lattices.
qd:039.difference: Saif & Gade's C->D switching is unconditional and applies to all cooperators; here it fires only for cooperators with at least 4 defector neighbours (interfaces), with strict-PD payoffs. The measured near-uniform state with noise-seeded bursts and a long correlation length is not reported in that form.
qd:039.citation_problems: arXiv 0910.0955 is cited without authors (Saif & Gade). Helbing & Yu concern success-driven migration, so they give weak support here.

qd:040.basis: The game-alone pattern is documented: with self-interaction, straight cooperator fronts invade for b<2 and stop at defector lines or fragments, which show local oscillations (Szabo & Fath 2007 sec. 6.5, Fig. 23); Newth & Cornforth report lines and blinkers at b=1.3 under synchronous updating.
qd:040.difference: No source couples Nowak-May with a conditional cooperator-biased conversion. The combination effect (thinner defector structures, higher dominance, fewer domains, longer correlation length) is not described.
qd:040.citation_problems: 'Sigmund, Univie notes' has no locatable reference. Newth & Cornforth's b=1.3 statement is unverified (paywalled). Stage 3's statement that rule 1 alone 'reproduces every feature' is wrong for this test: it differs from the full program beyond 3 robust spreads on n_domains (4.15 vs 3.14).

qd:044.basis: The pairwise couplings are documented: unconditional imitation plus voter copying (Vilone et al. 2014, 2012); payoff imitation plus conformity (Szolnoki & Perc 2015), including per-update probabilistic mixing of payoff-biased and conformist imitation in both PD and snowdrift on rings and scale-free networks (Pena, Volken, Pestelacci & Tomassini 2009, PRE 80:016110, found by reviewer).
qd:044.difference: No source combines all three update channels. The effect (voter noise preventing the fixation that majority plus game reaches and holding a ~90% state with minority islands) is not described; Pena et al. use rings and scale-free networks with stochastic payoff-biased imitation, not lattice imitate-best.
qd:044.citation_problems: Hauert & Doebeli misapplied: the prediction that defectors win comes from replicator-rule dynamics; under unconditional imitation the snowdrift lattice at T=1.5 favours cooperators (Roca et al. 2009).

qd:060.basis: No source describes it or a near relative. Distant relatives only: noise-perturbed Nowak-May lattices (Szabo & Fath review), and spatial PD players that themselves move by diffusion and chemotaxis (Burgess et al. 2017, J. Theor. Biol., seen in search results only), where the movers are the players rather than external agents flipping lattice states.
qd:060.difference: Not covered: external walkers that climb a gradient and flip lattice states coupled to a lattice game. Likely mechanism, from the sub-programs and code (census/sim.py: field starts at 1.0 with 20 low 3x3 patches plus small noise, no source term): agents gather at maxima of the decaying initial field, so their flips become localized and their activity decays, and imitate-best restores ordering. This probably decomposes into two known pieces and needs the further checks the label implies. Stage 3's claim that rule 1 is inert contradicts its own sub-program data: rules 2,3 give largest domain 0.34 vs 0.86 for the full program, and rules 1,2 give activity trend -3.53 vs 0.0001 for rule 2 alone.
qd:060.citation_problems: arXiv:0805.2071 is misattributed: the authors are Moyano & Sanchez, not 'Cuesta et al.' (the quoted 8+1 statement is in it). Hauert & Doebeli misapplied to imitate-best dynamics. Stage 3 ran no search on agent-driven perturbation, which it acknowledged.

review:016.basis: Nowak & May 1992 and Szabo & Fath 2007 (sec. 6.5): with self-interaction, 9/5<b<2 gives sustained competing invasions (spatial chaos) with cooperator density independent of the initial state; Wu, Fu & Wang (2023) prove finite lattices eventually cycle, so flipping persists. A defector-majority background is consistent with the Nowak-May cooperator fraction near 0.32.
review:016.citation_problems: No fabrication. The specific value '0.3178... for 1.8<T<2' could only be traced to a GitHub README in this check; it is consistent with the Nowak-May literature but unverified from the primary paper.

review:017.basis: Roca, Cuesta & Sanchez 2009 simulate this game (S=0.5, T=1.5) under unconditional imitation with synchronous and asynchronous updating on k=8 lattices, showing evolution to a mixed state (Figs. 18-19). Synchronous Nowak-May dynamics show local oscillating sites (Szabo & Fath sec. 6.5).
review:017.difference: No source explicitly reports site flip-backs for snowdrift imitate-best with probability-0.1 partial updating and self-interaction; Roca et al. report density trajectories only and omit self-interaction. Stage 3 read g=(1.5,0.5) as a PD with b=1.5, so its cited sources (Nowak-May spatial chaos, Huberman-Glance) describe a different game. The behaviour is near-trivial (g_reversals is 1.0 whenever any cell flips at two consecutive frames anywhere in the run).
review:017.citation_problems: Game misidentified: per the simulator, g=(T,S), so (1.5,0.5) is a snowdrift game, not PD b=1.5 (Stage 3 flagged the notation as an assumption). The Grilo & Correia citation merges two titles.

review:021.basis: Vilone et al. 2014: with unconditional imitation mixed with voter copying in the PD, a disordered active mixed state persists for high voter probability and low punishment, stable in the large-size limit; voter copying acts on interfaces.
review:021.difference: Vilone's active state is for the PD on random networks with a probabilistic choice between rules; here both rules act every step in sequence on a lattice in the snowdrift game, and the activity boost above either rule alone is not reported. Stage 3's mechanism (filament-like anti-coordinated snowdrift clusters) relies on replicator-rule results that do not hold for imitate-best.
review:021.citation_problems: arXiv:1102.4570 (Wang et al. 2011) does not contain the filament-cluster summary it is cited for. Cox-Durrett-Perkins treat weak voter-model perturbations in d>=3, not strong-selection imitate-best on a 2D lattice. Hauert & Doebeli used the replicator rule.

review:023.basis: Vilone et al. 2014 (PD, networks) and 2012 (coordination game, 2D lattices): mixing unconditional imitation with voter copying drives the system toward consensus.
review:023.difference: No source pairs voter copying with imitate-best in the snowdrift game; the voter-perturbation theory cited by Stage 3 assumes weak selection in d>=3. The measured partial ordering is not reported for this game.
review:023.citation_problems: JTB S0022519308001112 cited without authors (Szamado, Szalai & Scheuring 2008); its content could not be confirmed. Cox-Durrett-Perkins and Durrett 2014 assume weak selection in d>=3 (Stage 3 acknowledged this). This card duplicates qd:005.

review:037.basis: Payoff imitation plus conformity in the spatial PD: Cui & Wu 2013 (conformity plus payoff-biased transmission reaches high or full cooperation at low temptation), Szolnoki & Perc 2015 (surface tension, smooth interfaces), Lin et al. 2020 (combined rule always absorbed).
review:037.difference: None of these reports a persistent mixed state sustained by per-step majority adoption where imitate-best alone nearly fixes one strategy; the documented outcomes are cooperation enhancement or absorption, using a fixed conformist fraction or a combined Fermi-type rule.
review:037.citation_problems: Presenting Szolnoki & Perc's K=0.1 as matching the card's 0.1 is misleading: K is a noise temperature, not a conformity probability. Stage 3 verified sources through abstracts only (it says so).

review:041.basis: Roca, Cuesta & Sanchez 2009: under unconditional imitation on k=8 lattices, spatial structure fosters cooperation in the snowdrift game for T below ~1.7 (cooperator-dominated states with defector structures); Nowak-May-type flat-front invasion and local oscillations (Szabo & Fath).
review:041.difference: The count gate (cells with at most 2 type-0 neighbours never update) is not studied anywhere found; compared with ungated snowdrift imitate-best on other cards (largest domain ~0.82) it raises dominance. Stage 3 read the game as PD b~1.5 and explained the outcome with PD thresholds (b<1.8), which do not apply.
review:041.citation_problems: Game misidentified: g=(T,S)=(1.5,0.5) is a snowdrift game (census/sim.py), so the PD regime analysis and the 'cooperators take over for b<1.8' explanation do not apply (Stage 3 flagged the tuple mapping as unverified). The GitHub README is not a citable source.

review:042.basis: Nowak & May 1992: coexistence in fluctuating clusters at 1.8<b<2 under synchronous updating. Saif & Gade 2009 (J. Stat. Mech. P07023) study the same model with semi-synchronous updating (a fraction p of players per step, b=1.83, Moore+self).
review:042.difference: Saif & Gade find the ungated semi-synchronous model falls to all-defectors for p below ~0.87, so at p=0.1 the documented relative does not coexist. The gate (cells with 4 or more cooperating neighbours never update, which shields cooperator cores) is the likely reason coexistence persists here, and no source describes it. Stage 3's 'either outcome is documented' does not hold for the gated rule.
review:042.citation_problems: arXiv 0910.0961 is cited without authors (Saif & Gade), and its result (all-defector state at low update fraction) undercuts Stage 3's claim that the outcome does not matter.

review:054.basis: Nowak-May at b=1.3 relaxes to frozen or periodic cooperator-dominated patterns (Szabo & Fath sec. 6.5; Wu, Fu & Wang 2023). Conformity adds surface tension and smooth interfaces to payoff-driven lattice dynamics (Szolnoki & Perc 2015).
review:054.difference: The combination effect (rare per-step majority adoption accelerating the coarsening and activity decay of deterministic imitate-best) is not reported; Szolnoki & Perc use a fixed conformist fraction with Fermi updating on a k=4 lattice.
review:054.citation_problems: None fabricated. Stage 3 says each rule alone gives similar numbers, but both sub-programs differ from the full program beyond 3 robust spreads (n_domains, activity trend), so 'nothing new from the pair' is not supported by its own evidence.

review:056.basis: Sicardi et al. 2009: random dilution and mobility can suppress the inhibiting effect of spatial structure in the snowdrift game; Vainstein & Arenzon 2014: intermediate mobility can raise cooperation in PD and snowdrift under synchronous imitate-the-best.
review:056.difference: Their mobility uses empty sites on diluted von Neumann lattices; here neighbours swap on a full Moore+self lattice. Which type the swaps favour is not recorded on the card, so the match to 'mobility raises cooperation' is unconfirmed.
review:056.citation_problems: Hauert & Doebeli misapplied to imitate-best. Stage 3 noted the dilution-vs-swap difference but called it a rule difference only.

review:066.basis: Conformity-type majority adoption coupled with payoff imitation in the snowdrift region is studied by Szolnoki & Chen 2018 (square lattice) and Pena et al. 2009 (rings and scale-free networks).
review:066.difference: No source couples a strict-majority (7-of-8) switch with deterministic snowdrift imitate-best, and the rising-activity signature is not described anywhere found; Stage 3 gave no citation for its explanation that noise restarts imitation fronts.
review:066.citation_problems: Hauert & Doebeli misapplied to imitate-best dynamics. Stage 3 called the rising activity a slow transient, but it keeps its sign and more than half its size at 3x run length, which is the persistence criterion.

review:067.basis: The game-alone pattern (cooperator background with small defector clusters and oscillating sites at low b) is documented (Szabo & Fath sec. 6.5; blinkers for a nearby weak-PD payoff set in the SEP entry). One-way mutation noise in Nowak-May imitate-best is documented in the opposite direction (Saif & Gade: cooperators spontaneously defect with probability p).
review:067.difference: The D->C direction and its quantitative effects (fewer domains, slower activity decay) are not described. Nowak, Bonhoeffer & May 1994's abstract covers probabilistic transition rules and empty cells, not mutation.
review:067.citation_problems: Nowak, Bonhoeffer & May 1994 is cited for error/mutation variants that its abstract does not mention (Stage 3 marked it unverified).

census:g1:grid-25.basis: Near relative: Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007 document the coupling of cyclic dominance with exchange mobility (mobility enlarges and, above a critical value, destroys the spiral pattern) in the rate-based May-Leonard RPS model; Durrett-Neuhauser fast-stirring theory (via Durrett 1999) gives the general limit that strongly stirred particle systems approach mean-field reaction-diffusion behaviour. The CCA rule alone (4 colours, T=3, box) is documented by FGG 1991 and Shalizi & Shalizi (synchronous only).
census:g1:grid-25.difference: No source studies a threshold cyclic CA with stirring. The documented mobility effect is for a 3-species rate-based model with vacancies, where the outcome is an extinction transition, not partial pattern suppression with four types; the CCA part here is randomly updated, which the CCA sources do not cover; and the full program's reversal count exceeding both sub-programs (a non-additive feature) and its burstiness are not addressed anywhere. Stage 3's remark that these features are mostly stirring noise is plausible but is an interpretation, not a documented result.
census:g1:grid-25.citation_problems: Shalizi et al. citation misattributed (adds Haslinger and year 2004, conflating nlin/0507067 with the 2004 PRL). No citation addresses a threshold CCA with swaps; the KNOWN verdict rests on rule-by-rule sources plus a coupling documented only in a different cyclic model.

review:008.basis: Same rule with deterministic synchronous updating: the MCell lexicon (313 is the only significantly self-organising 3-colour range-1 CCA, with several spiral types) and FGG 1991 Fig. 8 ((1B,3,3) in the locally periodic spiral-equilibrium regime). The measured clustering and sustained cycling match that documented self-organisation qualitatively. Durrett (1992, J. Theor. Probab. 5:127-152) treats random cyclic colour models with threshold, but only in the large-range limit.
review:008.difference: The card's rule fires with probability 0.1 per step. No source documents the randomly updated threshold-3 CCA at range 1: FGG say stochastic counterparts of these threshold rules were not systematically studied and only conjecture that phenomena carry over, and the random-dynamics results that exist (cyclic particle system) are for threshold 1. Whether random updating keeps 313 in its spiral regime is therefore not established by any source.
review:008.citation_problems: Griffeath's 'four snapshots' is cited as a survey of randomly updated versions, but it treats the deterministic GH rule from random initial states (unsupportive for that claim). FGG's 'random processes' abstract sentence is generic; the paper explicitly does not study stochastic counterparts of threshold rules.

review:012.basis: Shalizi & Shalizi describe exactly this rule (4 colours, range-1 box, T=1, uniform random start; synchronous): every cell keeps cycling and the field departs only slightly from randomness as twisting single-colour bands. For the random-dynamics version, FGG 1991 (CCA in two dimensions, Sec. 3) report that the 2D threshold-1 cyclic particle system neither clusters nor fixates but settles into a stationary equilibrium of cycling wave formations whose scale grows with the number of colours (so small at 4 colours); Bello & Sivakoff 2021 restate that the threshold-1 CCA on Z^2 fluctuates for all kappa>=3. Both the synchronous limit and the random-dynamics class show the two measured features. Card note for the census team (not a literature issue): the reported activity 0.417 exceeds the 0.3 per-step maximum implied by the plain-words rule, so the activity measure or rule description should be checked.
review:012.citation_problems: Wikimedia Commons image category cited as a source (not evidentiary). Otherwise citations exist and are correctly described; Bramson-Griffeath and Fisch results quoted by Stage 3 are one-dimensional and only background.

review:015.basis: Near relatives: Gravner, Lyu & Sivakoff (arXiv:1610.07320, Theorem 6) prove that the 3-colour CCA/GHM with threshold 1 and synchronous updates oscillates on the giant component of an Erdos-Renyi graph G(n, lambda/n) with lambda>1. Bello & Sivakoff (2021, arXiv:2108.06404) study threshold >=2 CCA/GHM on regular trees and find a fluctuation/fixation transition near kappa*theta/d = 1 for large degree. Fretter, Lesne, Hilgetag & Hutt (arXiv:1403.6174) tie self-sustained threshold excitable activity on random graphs to cycle statistics. Reiter (2010, Computers & Graphics 34:72-76) runs threshold-1 CCA on non-lattice cell arrangements.
review:015.difference: The documented random-graph result is for threshold 1 and synchronous updating. For threshold 2 at mean degree about 4 with random updating no source establishes persistent cycling: Bello & Sivakoff state that fluctuation is open for small degrees, and their large-degree heuristic (kappa*theta/d = 6/3 > 1) points toward fixation on a 4-regular tree. Stage 3's appeal to lattice phase diagrams does not transfer to a sparse random graph.
review:015.citation_problems: One entry merges Durrett & Griffeath (1993) with 'Medley of spirals', which is Reiter (2010). The 'Gravner and Griffeath 1993' three-phase split quoted by Stage 3 concerns lattices; no cited source covers threshold 2 on random graphs.

review:045.basis: Near relative for the coupling: the three-candidate voter model under cyclic dominance (Tainaka & Itoh 1991; Szabo, Santos & Mendes 1999, PRE 60:3776, arXiv cond-mat/9907333) interpolates with a parameter P between neutral voter copying (P=1/2, coarsening to consensus) and cyclic invasion; for P>1/2 a self-organised domain pattern persists and the vortex density falls as a power of (P-1/2), so mixing in more voter copying enlarges the domains. Szabo & Szolnoki 2002 add an alignment (Potts) term to the cyclic voter model and report it shifts pattern formation toward spirals. The 313 rule alone is documented (MCell; FGG Fig. 8).
review:045.difference: The cyclic part here is the threshold-3, synchronous, deterministic 313 CCA, not threshold-1 rate-based invasion, and the copying is synchronous; no source combines voter copying with a threshold CCA, and the correlation-length and clustering changes are not reported for that pairing.
review:045.citation_problems: A GitHub code repository is cited as evidence. Szabo & Szolnoki 2002 is presented as covering voter copying, but its 'voter' is cyclic invasion and its addition is Potts energy. The closer relative (Tainaka-Itoh / Szabo-Santos-Mendes voter-cyclic interpolation) was not cited.

review:047.basis: Near relatives: in rate-based rock-paper-scissors, long-range links or small-world shortcuts synchronise local oscillations into global ones that end in extinction (Szabo, Szolnoki & Izsak 2004, J. Phys. A 37:2599; summarised in Szolnoki & Perc 2016, Sci. Rep. 6:38608), and exchange mobility above a critical value lets one species take over (Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007). Same general effect: long-range mixing of cyclic dominance drives near-takeover by one type.
review:047.difference: No source couples dissatisfaction-triggered (Schelling) relocation to random empty sites with a threshold cyclic CA in which the empty state is itself a member of the cycle; the documented routes use unconditional mobility or static shortcuts in rate-based RPS. Whether the dominant type rotates (global oscillation) or stays fixed was not measured, so the match to the documented global-oscillation route is unconfirmed. Reversals partly reflect relocation itself (Schelling-only 0.41).
review:047.citation_problems: PMC5137108 is labelled a review but is a research article (Szolnoki & Perc 2016); its intro does support the cited statement. arXiv:0710.3371 is unsupportive for this behaviour. No cited source involves Schelling-type relocation.

review:049.basis: Near relatives: mobility weakens cyclic spatial order in rate-based RPS lattice models; above a critical exchange rate coexistence and spirals are lost (Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007), and spirals survive only within a finite mobility window (Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny 2016). Same general effect (mixing reduces cyclic pattern order) in related models. The CCA rule alone is in FGG 1991 (synchronous).
review:049.difference: No source studies Schelling-type, dissatisfaction-triggered long-range relocation in a threshold cyclic CA, or a cycle containing the empty state; the documented mobility is unconditional nearest-neighbour exchange in rate-based models. The CCA part is randomly updated, which the CCA sources do not cover. Stage 3's 'turbulence/fixation boundary' placement uses 4-colour phenomenology; FGG Fig. 8 actually lists (1B,3,3) in the spiral-equilibrium regime.
review:049.citation_problems: Minor: author order for arXiv:1608.08932 given as Szczesny, Mobilia & Rucklidge (actual: Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny). No cited source involves Schelling-type relocation or a threshold CCA with mobility.

review:053.basis: Near relative with the same coupling: Demirel, Prizak, Reddy & Gross (2011, EPJ B 84:541; arXiv:1011.1124) couple 3-strategy RPS with rewiring of the loser to a random same-state node; with increasing rewiring probability the system passes through stationary and oscillatory phases with ongoing node and link dynamics, then frozen consensus and frozen fragmented phases. Choi, Xu & Hui (arXiv:1605.03370; EPJ B 2017) find an active connected phase and a frozen phase of three single-strategy clusters. Ongoing rewiring with continued but weakening state cycling matches the documented active regime and drift toward fragmentation.
review:053.difference: Four cyclic types (a 4-cycle has non-interacting neutral pairs; the documented adaptive models use 3 strategies), synchronous threshold-1 updating of every node applied independently of rewiring (in the documented models each discordant encounter yields either adoption or rewiring), and deterministic every-step rewiring. Whether this system is in a persistent active phase or slowly freezing was not determined.
review:053.citation_problems: None fabricated or misattributed. The sources document the coupling for 3 strategies only; Stage 3 cited the CCA family from memory.

review:060.basis: This is Griffeath's named rule 'Perfect' (R1/T3/C4/NM, MCell lexicon): from a random start it quickly forms a chaotic soup with a large length scale, and later widely separated spiral cores emerge and slowly take over. Shalizi & Shalizi (exactly 4 colours, range-1 box, T=3, synchronous, wrap-around lattice) describe this as metastable turbulence that spirals may or may not entrain on finite lattices; FGG 1991 list (1B,3,4) among rules that make very large perfect spirals. Large length scale and clustering are documented directly; the late-run fall in activity is consistent with this documented metastable relaxation on a small 64x64 lattice but is not reported as a measured quantity.
review:060.citation_problems: Shalizi & Shalizi misattributed to a five-author list (Shalizi, Haslinger, Rouquier, Klinkner, Moore). The FGG 'two dimensions' paper is cited for T=3 phenomenology that is actually in the companion threshold-range paper. Card-level note: feature label 'activity rising' but the measured trend is negative.

review:062.basis: Near relative with the same coupling type: in May-Leonard RPS with exchange mobility, spiral wavelength grows with mobility below a critical value (Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007), and the mobility rate shapes and can break up spirals (Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny 2016; Szolnoki et al. 2014 review). The longer correlation length matches that documented direction.
review:062.difference: The cyclic rule is a randomly updated threshold-3 CA without vacancies, not the rate-based May-Leonard model; no source studies a threshold CCA with swaps; the simultaneous fall in clustering and cycling with a rise in domain count is not covered; and the RMF robustness claim refers to the rate-based model family, not threshold rules.
review:062.citation_problems: No fabricated or misattributed citations. Stage 3 extends RMF's robustness statement to a threshold CCA, beyond what the paper covers.

review:064.basis: The CA part is documented: MCell 'Imperfect' (R1/T2/C4/NM) and Shalizi & Shalizi (T=2 spiral waves entrain the lattice). Near relative for the coupling: in May-Leonard RPS with exchange mobility, spiral wavelength rises with mobility up to a critical value (Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007; RMF 2008, J. Theor. Biol. 254:368), the same direction as the enlarged clustering here.
review:064.difference: No source couples a threshold CCA (deterministic, synchronous) with exchange; documented mobility effects are for rate-based 3-species models with vacancies. The halving of activity and the four-colour setting are not covered (the cited four-species work concerns rate-based models without this coupling).
review:064.citation_problems: None fabricated; Roman et al. journal reference unconfirmed (arXiv version exists). Stage 3 itself noted that no paper pairs CCA with swaps but still labelled KNOWN, which the frozen combination-effect definition does not allow.

review:069.basis: Rule 1 alone: the threshold-1 CCA on Z^2 fluctuates for kappa>=3 (FGG, restated by Bello & Sivakoff 2021), and its random-dynamics counterpart neither clusters nor fixates in 2D (FGG 1991, CCA in two dimensions). Near relative for the coupling: lattice RPS models with one altered transition keep coexistence with skewed abundances (Frean & Abraham 2001, Proc. R. Soc. B 268:1323; Avelino, de Oliveira & Trintin 2019, PRE 100:042209).
review:069.difference: Rule 2 is a spontaneous, contact-independent 0->1 conversion (a one-way mutation that seeds type 1 inside type-0 regions), not a change in the 1-invades-0 contact rate as Stage 3 asserts; the cited asymmetric-RPS papers alter predation/invasion probabilities. No source treats a threshold-1 cyclic CA with a one-directional spontaneous flip, and the changes in interface length and reversals are not covered.
review:069.citation_problems: arXiv:2108.06404 described as a 'CCA/GHM review' but is a research paper on regular trees whose introduction carries the Z^2 statement. Stage 3's mapping of the spontaneous flip onto a boosted invasion rate is incorrect, so the asymmetric-RPS papers support only a near relative.

census:g1:grid-6.basis: Gerin (2018) surveys exactly this SI 'Epidemic' probabilistic cellular automaton on a finite grid (spread without recovery) and its infinite-lattice counterpart, discrete-time Eden growth: with no recovery every site of a finite connected grid is eventually infected. Blavatska & Holovatch (2021) treat synchronous SI/SIS/SIR cellular automata on the square lattice (p = 1 is plain SI). The 8-neighbour neighbourhood and rate 0.1 are implementation details. Code check: fingerprint.py defines g_n_domains = log1p(number of clusters), confirming Stage 3's ln 2 = one-domain reading.

census:novelty:field-3.basis: Near relative: majority-vote CA = zero-temperature single-spin-flip Ising dynamics (Moore 1997) with curvature-driven coarsening and initial-density-dependent absorbing states (Bagnoli & Mencarelli 2026; Gaertner & Zehmakan, majority CA on the torus). These document the cell-level coarsening that the field copies.
census:novelty:field-3.difference: Every measured feature is a statistic of a write-only, non-decaying diffusing field (f_std, f_n_blobs). No source describes this readout, and its values depend on domain geometry, diffusion length and accumulation time, so they do not follow explicitly from any documented result. The cell process is documented; the field statistics are inferred. Field 1 and the 400 agents are inert.
census:novelty:field-3.citation_problems: No cited source addresses the emitted-field features. The ScienceDirect link could not be opened (403); its content matches Gaertner & Zehmakan.

census:novelty:grid-7.basis: Near relative: Oliveira's (1992) majority-vote model with noise, which is disordered above q_c = 0.075 on the square lattice. Walker flips (about 0.1 per cell per step) against majority updates (0.1) map to an effective q of about 1/3, deep in the disordered phase.
census:novelty:grid-7.difference: In Oliveira's model the noise is independent per site per update. Here it comes from a fixed number of persistent random walkers that flip cells along their trails, so it is correlated in space and time. No source treats walker-generated noise in majority-vote dynamics (2 targeted searches found none); the equivalence is an inference.

qd:045.basis: By the simulator's fixed initial conditions (sim.py: field 0 = 1 everywhere except 20 patches at 0.5 plus positive noise), field 0 exceeds 0.5 everywhere at step 1. Rule 2 therefore converts every type-0 cell to type 2 at once, and copying can never recreate type 0. The program is a 3-state voter model started from unequal densities. Documented: multi-state voter ordering from arbitrary initial configurations, including lattice simulations (Starnini et al. 2012); 2D voter coarsening without surface tension (Dornic et al. 2001; Tartaglia et al. 2015); and opinion-change counts that depend on initial concentrations (Ben-Naim et al. 1996). Voter dynamics conserve mean densities (exit probability = initial density), which gives the type count and entropy. The flip-back rise relative to the 4-state sub-program (0.76 vs 0.66) fits having fewer states but is not quantified in any source.

qd:046.basis: Near relative: 2D (multi-state) voter coarsening is documented (Dornic et al. 2001; Tartaglia et al. 2015; Starnini et al. 2012). The field mirrors those domains with no feedback.
qd:046.difference: All measured features are statistics of a write-only, accumulating field. No source describes them, and their values (std, blob count, spectral sharpness) depend on domain geometry, diffusion and accumulation time rather than following explicitly from a documented result. Field 0 is inert.

qd:050.basis: Near relatives: Schelling with vacancies, including its dependence on vacancy density and its frozen states (Gauvin, Vannimenus & Nadal 2009); an open-city Schelling model where an external reservoir sets agent density (Gauvin, Nadal & Vannimenus 2010).
qd:050.difference: Here agents of one type are created only at vacancies inside transient field patches, and relocation carries vacancies into these sinks until they are exhausted. No source describes this sink-driven vacancy exhaustion or its effect on domain count and churn. Stage 3's account is wrong on two points: it says the field starts random (sim.py: field 1 starts at 0 apart from 20 patches at 0.25), and it calls the effect a small one-off parameter shift, whereas the coupling removes nearly all vacancies.
qd:050.citation_problems: None fabricated. No cited source describes the field-sink/relocation coupling, and Stage 3's description of the field's initial state is incorrect.

qd:052.basis: Gray, Merkin, Needham & Scott (1990, Proc. R. Soc. A 430:509) and the Billingham & Needham series (1991) document cubic-autocatalysis travelling waves that carry the substrate state into the fully reacted autocatalyst state. With the simulator's initial fields (field 0 = 1, field 1 = 0 plus 1% noise and 20 seed patches), conversion is complete. The cell rule is a memoryless threshold readout with no feedback, so the all-type-1 endpoint follows directly and explicitly. It is a trivial absorbing outcome.
qd:052.citation_problems: Minor: rsta.1991.0098 is Part II of Billingham & Needham (immobilized autocatalyst); the unequal-diffusion travelling-wave results are in Part I (rsta.1991.0001).

qd:053.basis: Near relatives: 2-colour majority CA on the torus, whose final state depends on initial density (Gaertner & Zehmakan; Bagnoli & Mencarelli 2026, bifurcation by initial density), and zero-temperature q-state Potts coarsening from equal densities (Olejarz, Krapivsky & Redner 2013; Sire & Majumdar 1995).
qd:053.difference: No source treats majority/plurality dynamics with 3 states from an unequal composition, or the amplification of a dominant state under slow random updates. The documented biased-start results are for 2 colours with synchronous updates. Stage 3 offers Ising with globally conserved magnetization as an 'equivalent', but Sire & Majumdar use that mapping to describe correlations of one Potts state; it is conserved dynamics, the opposite of the amplification observed here.
qd:053.citation_problems: The Sire & Majumdar fixed-magnetization mapping is misapplied as documentation of an uneven starting composition; Krapivsky & Ben-Naim (1997) is about 1D.

qd:056.basis: Goles & Olivos (1980) and Poljak & Sura (1983, finite opinion sets) prove that synchronous symmetric majority dynamics end in fixed points or period-2 cycles. This documents the flip-back component of the majority sub-program.
qd:056.difference: The full-program value depends on all three rules: rules 2+3 give 0.80 and the full program 0.58 (about 19 robust spreads apart), so heading alignment among the agents matters once agents perturb the majority CA. Stage 3 says alignment 'changes almost nothing', which its own sub-program table contradicts. No source describes a majority CA perturbed by mobile or aligning agents (2 targeted searches); the period-2 theorem covers only the unperturbed rule.
qd:056.citation_problems: Stage 3's statement that rule 1 changes almost nothing is contradicted by the rules-2,3 vs full comparison on its own card.

qd:057.basis: Near relatives: in Schelling-Ising models, noise is needed for large-domain segregation (Stauffer & Schulze 2007: zero noise gives no large domains, small nonzero noise gives ghettos); Schelling with spontaneous Glauber and Kawasaki perturbations (Barret & Torri 2023); statistical physics of Schelling coarsening (Dall'Asta et al. 2008).
qd:057.difference: Here the perturbation is non-conservative and directed: it creates and destroys agents cyclically, cutting vacancy density from 1/3 to about 0.12. It is delivered along walker trails and modulated by walker-walker repulsion. No source covers this kind of noise or the dependence on repulsion. Stage 3's caveat is resolved: the large domain is an agent type, not vacancies.
qd:057.citation_problems: Misattribution: arXiv:0710.5237 is Stauffer & Schulze (2007), not Stauffer & Solomon.

qd:064.basis: Hartarsky & Lichev (arXiv:2501.18976) state that threshold 4 on the 3x3 box (their 'square-diagonal' model) is the smallest critical threshold, via the universality results of Bollobas, Duminil-Copin, Morris & Smith. The critical density on an n x n torus therefore vanishes, and a fixed density of 0.5 fills it; at p = 0.5, 64% of type-1 cells already have at least 4 type-0 neighbours. Uniform emission over a uniform lattice gives a uniform, linearly growing field (explicit arithmetic). This is a trivial absorbing outcome plus bookkeeping.
qd:064.citation_problems: Reasoning slip, not a citation problem: Stage 3 read the rule-1-only f_mean of 0.9833 as the type-0 fraction. It is the untouched initial field 0 (1 everywhere except 20 patches at 0.5), because nothing emits in that sub-program. The fill is instead confirmed by the full program's f_mean being twice the knock-out.

qd:071.basis: No rule reads a field, so the cell dynamics are exactly the Schelling sub-program, whose rapid early relaxation and interface shortening are documented (Gauvin et al. 2009: large clusters form within about 10 steps; Vinkovic & Kirman 2006; Dall'Asta et al. 2008). I reran the full program with the project simulator: steps_run = 6 and unstable = True, vs 1000 steps for Schelling alone. This explains why the 3x-run-length differences equal the original ones exactly (-1.5028 and -0.1341 in verify.json) and why g_n_domains barely moves.
qd:071.citation_problems: Stage 3's explanation of the full-vs-rule-2 gap is wrong. It suggested the activity measure counts field changes or that random-number streams shift, but grid activity counts only cell changes (filter.py) and rules 1 and 3 draw no random numbers. The cause is the numerical blow-up and truncated run. arXiv:1505.00429 does not support the lattice-coarsening statement attributed to the cited sources.

review:011.basis: Near relatives: the rewiring-only (phi -> 1) limit of the Holme-Newman model, where communities equal the initial opinion groups and components become random graphs; graph fission in the rewire-to-same evolving voter model (Durrett et al. 2012).
review:011.difference: In those models every node rewires, so each opinion group stays connected: about 2 components plus a few isolated nodes, i.e. log1p about 1.6-1.9. Here rewiring is one-sided, so the non-rewiring group is abandoned and fragments according to Erdos-Renyi component statistics at mean degree about 2. I found no source on one-sided rewiring; asymmetric coevolving-voter work (Wieland & Nunes 2013) uses different strategies. Stage 3 read N[0] as 'every node' and the log-scaled 2.92 as a raw count of components, so its sources do not describe the measured value.
review:011.citation_problems: The cited sources describe symmetric rewiring, and the measured value contradicts the symmetric case. The last citation cannot be identified.

review:018.basis: Holme & Newman 2006 (copying plus rewiring to same-opinion nodes, many opinions, final opinion-pure components); Vazquez, Eguiluz & San Miguel 2008 (active-to-frozen fragmentation transition, finite-network value near p about 0.38 for mean degree 4; here the effective rewiring share is about 0.5); Boehme & Gross 2011 and 2012 (fragmentation transitions, analytical three-opinion case). Extra rewiring from copying-created active links is a direct consequence of the documented coupling. Synchronous copying is an implementation difference; this run sits where the documented phase diagram puts it.

review:019.basis: Holme & Newman 2006; Vazquez et al. 2008 (below the transition: a single component reaching consensus); Durrett et al. 2012 (rewire-to-same transition); Boehme & Gross (three-opinion fragmentation). At an effective rewiring share of about 0.09 the documented outcome is consensus, and continued rewiring of active links before consensus follows directly from the coupling.
review:019.citation_problems: Minor: Shi, Mucha & Durrett's multi-opinion results are for rewire-to-random, not rewire-to-same.

review:025.basis: Near relatives: the Schelling-Voter model (Caridi et al. 2013, 2017), where unhappy agents move or change state and extinction of one state is among the stationary outcomes; freezing of zero-temperature Potts dynamics on the square lattice (Chippari & Picco).
review:025.difference: Here state change is an unconditional synchronous plurality rule applied to every cell including vacancies, so the empty type can win, and relocation is to random vacancies. No source describes relocation shortening or securing fixation of this rule within the run. Stage 3's key support ('straight interfaces ... unstable in majority rule. Thus consensus is always achieved', Redner 2019) describes the group majority-rule model, where whole neighbourhoods adopt their majority: a different model. Makowiec (2004) concerns rewiring of a network, not lattice relocation.
review:025.citation_problems: Redner 2019 is misapplied: the consensus statement concerns a different 'majority rule' model. Makowiec 2004 is a network model.

review:026.basis: Near relatives: noisy Schelling (Gauvin et al. 2009: satisfied agents also move, which adds noise; mixed states where the system keeps oscillating between configurations); Schelling with spontaneous Kawasaki (swap) perturbations (Barret & Torri 2023); Dall'Asta et al. 2008.
review:026.difference: Here the noise is unconditional nearest-neighbour exchange at every step (infinite-temperature Kawasaki), and movers go to random rather than satisfying vacancies. The one combination feature (flip-back share 0.94) is a cell-level churn statistic that no source describes for this or an equivalent coupling.

review:027.basis: Same general effect in related models: Gauvin et al. (2009) state that noise from satisfied agents' moves avoids large-but-finite cluster states, so large-scale segregation occurs; Stauffer & Schulze (2007) find noise is needed for large domains; Barret & Torri (2023) treat Schelling with Kawasaki swap perturbations.
review:027.difference: The noise mechanism differs: random nearest-neighbour exchange here, vs satisfied agents moving to satisfying vacancies (Gauvin) or temperature-controlled moves. Unhappy agents here relocate to random vacancies. The flip-back enhancement is not described anywhere. g_moran is computed on numeric type labels.

review:028.basis: Near relative: the Schelling-Voter model (Caridi et al. 2013, 2017), where unhappy agents on a 2D lattice either move or switch state; 2D voter coarsening (Tartaglia et al.; Dornic et al.).
review:028.difference: In the Schelling-Voter model only unhappy agents act and vacancies are not copied. Here copying is unconditional and synchronous, and it spreads vacancies. No source describes the flip-back or spectral-peak combination; the spectral peak may be an update-scheme or trend artifact (not verified).

review:034.basis: Near relative: the four-species cyclic Lotka-Volterra model on the square lattice (Szabo & Sznaider 2004), where neutral pairs form defensive alliances whose domains grow and coarsen until one alliance fills the lattice.
review:034.difference: In Szabo & Sznaider, alliance partners mix through vacancies and invasion is strict predation. Here there are no vacancies, an activated cell copies any random neighbour (not only its successor), and alliance domains are frozen mosaics of the two neutral types. No source describes this gated-copy rule. Stage 3 identified the rule as the plain multi-state voter model, claiming the gate 'only removes copies that would change nothing'. The simulator code shows that is false: NEXT_GE counts neighbours equal to (own type + 1) mod k. Its voter citations therefore do not describe this system; this is the known recognise-the-family failure mode.
review:034.citation_problems: All five Stage 3 citations concern the voter model, which this cyclic-gated rule is not; the identification is wrong.

review:036.basis: Voter model on networks: densities are martingales performing a random walk to consensus, with mean consensus time proportional to N mu1^2/mu2 (Sood & Redner 2005); multi-state voter mean-field consensus time and exit probabilities (Starnini et al. 2012).
review:036.citation_problems: Stage 3 took the substrate to be a 2D square lattice with 4 neighbours, but the N layer is a random network (sim.py: Erdos-Renyi, mean degree 4) and kN=4 is the number of states. Its lattice-specific sources and claims (1/ln t interface decay, L^2 log L consensus time) do not apply; the label rests on network-voter sources instead.

review:052.basis: Fu & Wang 2008 (PRE 78, 016104) study the coupled system: majority-preference opinion updating plus minority-avoidance rewiring toward like-minded nodes, with many opinions. When majority updating dominates, a uniform opinion is reached, so discordant links and the rewiring they trigger vanish; the lower turnover follows directly. Holme & Newman 2006 for the rewiring mechanism. The rewiring target differs: a random same-type node here, vs a same-opinion neighbour-of-neighbour or a random node in Fu & Wang.
review:052.citation_problems: arXiv:1403.6106 is misattributed (Carro, Vazquez, Toral & San Miguel, not Fernandez-Gracia et al.) and treats link-state, not node-state, majority dynamics, so it is not the 'closest documented match' Stage 3 claims.

review:057.basis: Near relatives: Schelling at high vacancy density (diluted segregated phase, Gauvin et al. 2009); Schelling with switching agents (Hazan & Randon-Furling 2013); generic Schelling relaxation.
review:057.difference: Here one population decays to extinction, so the late system has a single agent type. That is not the two-type diluted phase Stage 3 invoked ('two-type Schelling at about 67% vacancy'). The measured features come from the decay transient followed by freezing. No source describes Schelling dynamics under decay of one population to extinction (searched). Stage 3's 0/0-share caveat is settled by the code: isolated agents are happy.
review:057.citation_problems: The diluted-phase match rests on a misidentification: after the decay only one agent type remains.

review:058.basis: Near relatives: Schelling with blind relocation to random vacancies and frozen all-satisfied states (Singh et al. 2007; Abella et al. 2022); open-city Schelling where agents leave or enter through a reservoir (Gauvin, Nadal & Vannimenus 2010).
review:058.difference: Removal here is random decay of one type to extinction, not utility-driven exit, and the measured features are transient churn statistics. No source describes this combination (searched).

review:063.basis: Near relatives: the Schelling-Voter model (Caridi et al. 2013, 2017), with extinction of one state among its outcomes; Schelling at very low tolerance staying disordered or frozen (Gauvin et al. 2009).
review:063.difference: Here state change is unconditional majority adoption applied at a low rate to every cell, there are three agent types, and relocation to random vacancies acts as stirring. The synergy, where neither rule alone lowers entropy but together they do, is not described in any source.

review:068.basis: Near relatives: polluted bootstrap percolation, where closed sites shield empty sites and growth stalls (definition as in Gravner & Holroyd 2017; the 2D case is Gravner & McDonald); Schelling frozen states without accommodating vacancies (Dall'Asta et al. 2008).
review:068.difference: No source couples threshold growth with relocating blockers (targeted search found none). The vacancy exhaustion comes from relocation re-placing vacancies at random until each one meets the growth threshold. Stage 3 conceded it found no such paper and argued 'missing rule combination, not missing behaviour', which is exactly what the study's definition excludes. Stage 3 also said rule 2 moves only type-2 cells; it moves all agents (types 1 and 2, counts conserved), though the conclusion that the lost type is the empty one still holds.
review:068.citation_problems: None fabricated, but no citation covers the combination.

census:g1:agents-1.basis: This is Strombom's Local Attraction Model with synchronous update in the strong-attraction limit (the code replaces the heading with the direction to the local centre, so c is effectively above the studied range). Strombom et al. 2019 (PMC full text) state that for c in [1.7, 2] relatively stationary swarms form with very low polarization; Strombom 2011 introduces the swarm phase. Clustering and near-zero displacement are documented. The negative local alignment is not stated in a source but follows from agents heading toward a common local centre inside a stationary aggregate.

census:g1:agents-2.basis: Negi, Iyer & Gompper 2024 (Sci Rep 14:9443, arXiv:2402.03851) simulate active particles whose only interaction is a visual torque steering them away from neighbours (no alignment; the vision half-angle theta=pi gives all-round vision). They report that diffusion is 'strongly reduced for large maneuverability' (D ~ Pe^2/Omega for theta=pi). This program is the infinite-maneuverability, all-round-vision, discrete-time limit of that mechanism at higher density (Phi = N(R/L)^2 = 9 vs at most 2.5), so the suppressed displacement is documented for an equivalent system. Stage 3's own sources do not document it.
census:g1:agents-2.citation_problems: None of Stage 3's three citations addresses the measured feature (suppressed displacement). arXiv:1301.6294 is an alignment-plus-repulsion Vicsek variant (Romenskyy & Lobaskin), not a repulsion-only model. The label rests on Negi et al. 2024, found by the reviewer.

census:g1:agents-3.basis: The rule is the 1995 Vicsek model. Gregoire & Chate 2004 describe the disordered phase at and below threshold as nucleated ordered patches, and density waves near onset; the Chatterjee essay summarises Vicsek's clusters at low density and noise and the band coexistence regime; Bai & Le 2026 report dense locally ordered bands in an intermediate regime. Weak local order with density clustering is standard near-transition Vicsek phenomenology. The large speed (v=1) shifts the transition point but not the kind of behaviour.
census:g1:agents-3.citation_problems: The Chatterjee essay is an unrefereed course paper (secondary). Otherwise none.

census:g1:agents-8.basis: Trivial single-agent outcome, documented: Cornejo-Olea et al. 2025 show trapping of Brownian gradient-ascent trajectories at local and secondary maxima of a fixed landscape; Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021 show particles aggregating and staying at the maximum of an imposed constant attractant; Johnston & Painter 2019 (abstract) describe local gradient-followers localising at peaks of rough terrain. Stage 3 read the field correctly as passive (verified: no emission rule; field 0 = 1 with twenty 0.5 patches plus 1% noise, diffusion only).
census:g1:agents-8.citation_problems: arXiv:1202.2442 is used for a sentence that refers to self-generated attractant with receptor saturation (partial support only).

census:g1:network-phase-2.basis: Near relatives. Dorrian, Borresen & Amos 2013: Kuramoto on community-structured networks, where clusters synchronise internally while the global order parameter oscillates. Gleiser & Zanette 2006, and prior work summarised in Papadopoulos et al. 2017: coherence-based adaptive rewiring makes synchronized groups coincide with network clusters (modular, local rather than global synchrony). Cardenas-Sabando et al. 2026: rewiring by fixed node states fragments the network at extreme homophily (rule 2 alone).
census:g1:network-phase-2.difference: No source couples Kuramoto dynamics with rewiring driven by fixed type labels unrelated to phase or frequency. Here the modules become fully disconnected (Dorrian's clusters keep sparse links and the oscillation there needs them), and the fluctuating global order comes from independent components locked at different mean frequencies. Each rule alone is documented and the combined result is a short, near-trivial chain, but no source describes the combined behaviour; Stage 3 itself said it found no paper with this setup. Under the frozen combination rule this is CLOSELY RELATED, not DOCUMENTED.
census:g1:network-phase-2.citation_problems: Papadopoulos et al. 2017 is cited for 'adaptive rewiring -> modular organization, local not global synchrony', which is the opposite of its own result (its rule rewires in-phase links and raises global synchrony); the modular statement appears in its text only as a summary of prior work.

census:novelty:agents-16.basis: A reviewer rerun of census/sim.py (seed 0, step 600) gives heading minus gradient angle = 90.0 degrees for every agent before noise. So this is exact transverse (contour-following) taxis, not a chiral circle swimmer whose rotation competes with chemotaxis as Stage 3 described: the heading is reset to the gradient each step before the turn. Near relatives: Maity & Burada 2022 (a chiral swimmer in a chemical gradient can be trapped in closed orbits near the source); Geiseler et al. 2016 (chiral swimmers show transverse chemotaxis across travelling waves); contour-following steering in control-theory and C. elegans klinotaxis models (search results).
census:novelty:agents-16.difference: No source studies agents locked at exactly 90 degrees to the gradient of a passive multi-peak field, or reports the resulting population-level partial clustering. Maity & Burada treat one swimmer near one source with slip-modulated steering; Geiseler et al. treat travelling waves.
census:novelty:agents-16.citation_problems: Stage 3 mischaracterised the mechanism: it treated rule 2 as a constant chirality competing with gradient ascent, but the turn is applied after a full heading reset, giving pure transverse taxis. Its sources describe chiral swimmers and traps, near relatives at best.

census:novelty:agents-17.basis: Near relatives. Taktikos, Zaburdaev & Stark 2012: walkers steered toward a chemical gradient, with harmonic repulsion, form bound clusters of limited size, but the field is self-generated. Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021: particles with soft-core repulsion (and aligning collisions) aggregate around the maximum of an externally imposed attractant. Program spec checked in census/runs/verify/inventory.json and census/sim.py: the field starts at 1.0 (field 0) or 0 (field 1) with twenty 3x3 patches (0.5 / 0.25) plus 1% noise and only diffuses; the program has no emission or deposit rule; A.CLIMB sets the heading to the local gradient direction. The knock-out differs from the full program because census/knockout.py removes A.CLIMB, which reads the field. Stage 3's inference of hidden emission is therefore wrong.
census:novelty:agents-17.difference: Stage 3's mechanism (Keller-Segel autochemotactic collapse arrested by repulsion) does not apply: collapse with rule 1 alone is gradient trapping on a passive landscape. No source combines pure turn-away repulsion with gradient climbing on a fixed multi-peak landscape, or reports the measured partial clustering with anti-aligned neighbours.
census:novelty:agents-17.citation_problems: All Stage 3 citations describe self-generated (autochemotactic) fields. The program has no emission, so none of them describes this system. Stage 3 inferred emission from the knock-out, but the knock-out differs because it removes the field-reading A.CLIMB rule.

census:novelty:agents-8.basis: Near relatives. Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021: with an external attractant and aligning collisions, particles aggregate at the maximum, alignment speeds aggregation, and inside aggregates particles mostly tumble or halt. Romanczuk et al. 2012 review (full text): adding velocity alignment to chemotactic clustering produces 'collective rotation within a stationary cluster', which the authors say corresponds to dynamics in an external central field. Program spec checked in census/runs/verify/inventory.json and census/sim.py: the field starts at 1.0 (field 0) or 0 (field 1) with twenty 3x3 patches (0.5 / 0.25) plus 1% noise and only diffuses; the program has no emission or deposit rule; A.CLIMB sets the heading to the local gradient direction. The knock-out differs from the full program because census/knockout.py removes A.CLIMB, which reads the field. Stage 3's inference of hidden emission is therefore wrong.
census:novelty:agents-8.difference: No source reports point-like, strongly polar-aligned but stationary clumps at the maxima of a fixed multi-peak landscape. Chatterjee & Goldenfeld's aggregates are not aligned and include repulsion; the review's aligned stationary clusters form in a self-generated field and rotate. Stage 3's autochemotaxis framing is wrong for this program.
census:novelty:agents-8.citation_problems: All four Stage 3 citations concern self-generated chemical fields. Stage 3 inferred hidden emission from the knock-out, but the knock-out differs only because it removes the field-reading A.CLIMB rule.

census:novelty:field-1.basis: No rule reads field 0 (verified in the program spec), so the field features are a diffusion-smoothed time integral of agent density and cannot reflect anything the agents are not doing. The agent-level behaviour, coherent groups and density inhomogeneity at low noise relative to neighbour count, is documented: Vicsek 1995 (via the Chatterjee essay), Gregoire & Chate 2004, Ginelli 2016, Duan et al. 2026. The 'combination effect' only means deposition is needed to make the agent pattern visible. Labelled DOCUMENTED under the trivial-outcome clause, treating the passive field as an observable of an equivalent system.

census:novelty:grid-8.basis: No rule reads the cells, so cell activity is a readout of agent positions: trapped agents occupy few distinct cells, and repeated flips cancel between frames recorded every 2 steps. Trapping of gradient climbers at local maxima of a fixed landscape is documented (Cornejo-Olea et al. 2025; Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021). Reversal of a two-state flip on revisit is an identity (Langton's-ant cell rule). DOCUMENTED as a trivial readout of a documented agent behaviour.
census:novelty:grid-8.citation_problems: Stage 3's 'two agents on one cell in the same step flip it twice and cancel' is impossible in the code: A.WRITECELL advances each occupied cell once per step (np.unique). The cancellation that matters is between recorded frames. The Nature citation could not be verified.

qd:027.basis: Same near relatives as census:novelty:agents-8. Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021 (cited by Stage 3, quote verified): aggregation at the maximum of an external attractant, helped by aligning interactions. Romanczuk et al. 2012: alignment plus chemotactic clustering gives collective rotation in stationary clusters. Program spec checked in census/runs/verify/inventory.json and census/sim.py: the field starts at 1.0 (field 0) or 0 (field 1) with twenty 3x3 patches (0.5 / 0.25) plus 1% noise and only diffuses; the program has no emission or deposit rule; A.CLIMB sets the heading to the local gradient direction. The knock-out differs from the full program because census/knockout.py removes A.CLIMB, which reads the field. Stage 3's inference of hidden emission is therefore wrong.
qd:027.difference: No source reports dense, nearly immobile clumps that stay strongly aligned at the maxima of a fixed multi-peak landscape, or the raised fluctuation of global polarization. Chatterjee & Goldenfeld's aggregates are not aligned; the other relatives use self-produced signals.
qd:027.citation_problems: Three of Stage 3's four citations concern self-produced signals; this program has no emission.

qd:033.basis: A reviewer rerun of census/sim.py gives heading minus gradient angle = 90.0 degrees for every agent before noise. Near relatives as for census:novelty:agents-16: Maity & Burada 2022 (orbital states of a chiral swimmer around a chemical source) and Geiseler et al. 2016 (transverse chemotaxis of chiral swimmers). Program spec checked in census/runs/verify/inventory.json and census/sim.py: the field starts at 1.0 (field 0) or 0 (field 1) with twenty 3x3 patches (0.5 / 0.25) plus 1% noise and only diffuses; the program has no emission or deposit rule; A.CLIMB sets the heading to the local gradient direction. The knock-out differs from the full program because census/knockout.py removes A.CLIMB, which reads the field. Stage 3's inference of hidden emission is therefore wrong.
qd:033.difference: Stage 3 misread both rules: the cells have one type, not a random checkerboard of left and right turns acting as noise, and there is no emission, so this is not autochemotaxis. No source describes exact 90-degree transverse taxis in a passive landscape, or the emergent alignment of co-circulating agents.
qd:033.citation_problems: Stage 3's sources describe autochemotactic or interacting particles; the program has neither emission nor agent-agent interaction, and Stage 3 misdescribed rule 2.

qd:036.basis: No rule reads field 0 (verified), so the features are a time-integrated readout of agent density. Barberis 2018 shows that the Vicsek model at very low noise forms a single macroscopic cluster, and Vicsek 1995 (via the Chatterjee essay) shows clusters at low density and low noise; this parameter point (noise 0.3 rad) is in that regime. DOCUMENTED under the trivial-outcome clause, as for census:novelty:field-1.

qd:041.basis: Passive readout of documented trapping, as for census:novelty:grid-8: cells are never read, trapped agents flip few distinct cells, and flips cancel between frames. Gradient trapping is documented (Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021; Cornejo-Olea et al. 2025). The high CV is a small-mean statistic of the same readout (it halves at 4x area, where there are more agents, and grows at 3x run length). Stage 3 correctly noted that the knock-out's zero baseline is uninformative and that writing alone is the fair baseline.
qd:041.citation_problems: Stage 3's 'same-step toggles cancel' mechanism is wrong for this code (each occupied cell is advanced once per step); otherwise the cited Chatterjee & Goldenfeld quote is accurate.

qd:065.basis: Near relatives for the transient: Chatterjee & Goldenfeld 2021 (aggregation in an imposed attractant field); Stocker et al. 2008 PNAS 105:4209 (chemotactic accumulation in ephemeral, dissipating nutrient patches forms short-lived hot spots); Geiseler et al. 2016 (non-adaptive swimmers in travelling chemical waves). A reviewer rerun of census/sim.py (seed 0) shows field 0 almost fully consumed by step 100 (field 1 mean 0.986). Its median gradient is about 1e-26 at step 100 and 1e-191 at step 300. Field 0 underflows to exactly 0 everywhere by step 500, after which A.CLIMB leaves headings unchanged and the zero-noise agents move ballistically in frozen co-moving groups. The late-window values (and the 3x run-length values) therefore measure a degenerate state created by floating-point underflow.
qd:065.difference: No source covers gradient-climbing agents in an attractant consumed by an autocatalytic reaction. More importantly, the robust features are measured after the attractant has vanished numerically, so they are an artifact (Stage 3's suggested gradient check, run by the reviewer, confirms this), not a behaviour any source could document. Recommend treating it as an artifact and excluding it; CLOSELY RELATED applies only to the transient.
qd:065.citation_problems: Two of Stage 3's three citations are non-peer-reviewed web pages that support only the reaction term.

review:009.basis: 'N kN=1' is the network layer (census/sim.py: Erdos-Renyi graph, NN=200, mean degree 4; verify inventory view 'N.phase'), not a lattice. Gomez-Gardenes, Moreno & Arenas 2007 show that on ER networks the Kuramoto order parameter rises from zero above a critical coupling (partial synchronization), alongside a growing fraction of frequency-synchronized links; reviews: Arenas et al. 2008, Rodrigues et al. 2016. Random gating scales the natural-frequency and coupling terms by the same factor, and Jeter & Belykh 2015 show that fast stochastic on-off switching is governed by the averaged network. Partial phase order with frequency entrainment is the documented behaviour; the rise of r with run length is slow convergence.
review:009.citation_problems: Stage 3 analysed the program as a 2-D nearest-neighbour lattice. Its lattice sources (Hong-Park-Choi 2005; arXiv 2004.00294, 1011.5823, 1512.02335) and its vortex-coarsening explanation of the size and run-length trends do not apply to this random-graph system. The label holds through network sources found by the reviewer.

review:046.basis: Szabo & Szolnoki 2002, 'A three-state cyclic voter model extended with Potts energy', PRE 65:036115 (arXiv cond-mat/0110255). Adding Potts interfacial energy (surface tension, the stochastic counterpart of majority smoothing) to three-state cyclic invasion on a square lattice cuts the vortex density sharply: the power-law exponent in P goes from 0.29 at K=0 to 2.05 at K=1. Evolution then becomes 'governed by spiral formation' with smooth, rotating spiral arms (Fig. 5), in place of the small irregular domains (xi~2.5) of pure cyclic invasion. Szolnoki, Szabo & Ravasz 2005, 'Three-state Potts model in combination with the rock-scissors-paper game', PRE 71:027102 (cond-mat/0407322), a paper citing the first: cyclic dominance destroys the Potts ordering transition and sustains a self-organizing pattern with rotating spiral arms even at low temperature. That is, the coarsening/ordering of the smoothing-only system is replaced by persistent rotating spirals, the same contrast as majority-only vs full program here. The Szabo & Fath 2007 review (Phys Rep 446) restates that rotating spiral arms become visible when invasion fronts feel a surface tension. A CA-side relative is Gerhardt, Schuster & Tyson 1990 (excitable CA with neighbourhood averaging giving curvature effects and rotating waves).
review:046.difference: The documented models are stochastic, sequential Monte Carlo models: pairwise invasion weighted by a Potts energy, on nearest-neighbour lattices. Here the smoothing is a separate deterministic, synchronous Moore-majority step (zero temperature, random tie-break) and the invasion is the deterministic threshold-1 cyclic CA. That cyclic rule's own baseline is a frozen near-random texture cycling with global period 3 (Shalizi & Shalizi), not the dynamic small-domain state of stochastic rock-paper-scissors. No source reports this deterministic-CA realisation or its numbers (rotation period ~10 steps, ~40-48 vortices per 64x64, correlation length 3). No new kind of behaviour was found beyond the documented 'surface tension + cyclic invasion -> coarse rotating spirals' effect. The label is borderline DOCUMENTED: it was kept at CLOSELY RELATED only because the update scheme is not equivalent. Stage 3 got the mechanism wrong in two ways. First, period-2 blinking from synchronous majority cannot produce the reversals, because period-2 cycles are invisible at the census's even (10-step) frame spacing. Second, spirals are present, not suppressed.
review:046.citation_problems: Nothing fabricated or misattributed. Goles-Olivos and Poljak-Sura are correct but misapplied: they are used to explain reversals of 0.94 as synchronous period-2 blinking, which cannot register at the census's 10-step frame spacing. The reversals come from aliasing of a ~10-step spiral rotation. The MCell lexicon quote could not be verified because the site is offline.

review:050.basis:
Near relatives cover each half of the coupling and the general effect.
(i) Cyclic dominance plus mobility: Reichenbach, Mobilia & Frey 2007 (Nature 448:1046) and Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny 2016 (Games 7:24). Mobility reshapes and breaks up the cyclic patterns, and coherent spirals exist only in a finite mobility window.
(ii) Schelling dynamics with agents whose type changes: Hazan & Randon-Furling 2013 (EPJ B 86:421), where fixed agents switching type stop segregation from completing and give mixed patches with fuzzy interfaces; and Caridi et al. 2017 (Physica A 487:125), the Schelling-Voter model, where an unhappy agent either moves or changes type.
(iii) Long-range links in rock-scissors-paper synchronize local oscillations into a global oscillation (Szabo, Szolnoki & Izsak 2004, J Phys A; Szolnoki & Szabo 2004, PRE, arXiv cond-mat/0407425). That is the same general effect the random long-range relocation appears to produce here.
review:050.difference:
No source found couples an excitable or cyclic CA with Schelling-type relocation triggered by dissatisfaction and sent to random empty cells. The cyclic CA here is the threshold-1 Moore CCA, whose own state is the incoherent period-4 'quench'. No source has the vacant state inside the colour cycle either, which here means the cycle creates and destroys vacancies and the cells agents move into are themselves cycling.
Not covered is the specific outcome: clustering above the Schelling-only level while about 60% of cells keep changing, i.e. segregated blocks that cycle colour together.
Two further features showed up in the reviewer re-run but are not among the verified features, so they need a follow-up check before any claim is made: a large-amplitude whole-lattice composition oscillation, and an asymmetric time-averaged composition (type 2 ~0.41, the others ~0.17-0.22). Only two of the three verified features clearly need both rules: the domain-count change is within one robust spread of Schelling alone.
review:050.citation_problems: Nothing fabricated. Minor problems: the author order of the 2016 Games paper is wrong (it is Mobilia, Rucklidge, Szczesny). Fisch-Gravner-Griffeath 1991 and Durrett-Griffeath 1993 are cited for a wave/'demon'-dominated threshold-1 state that does not apply to the 4-colour Moore range-1 rule, which is documented as the incoherent 'quench'. 'Random relocation' is not Schelling's 1971 move rule.

review:051.basis:
The near relatives are the same as for review:050.
The cyclic rule alone is the documented threshold-1 Moore 'quench', with the whole lattice cycling (Shalizi & Shalizi, nlin/0507067: 4 colours, box neighbourhood, random start, the same set-up as here).
Schelling dynamics kept active by agents that change type: Hazan & Randon-Furling 2013, with fixed switching agents giving mixed patches and fuzzy interfaces; and Caridi et al. 2017, the Schelling-Voter model, where an unhappy agent moves or changes type.
Mobility in cyclic dominance changes or breaks the patterns: Reichenbach et al. 2007; Mobilia, Rucklidge & Szczesny 2016.
Long-range interactions synchronize cyclic oscillations into a global oscillation: Szabo, Szolnoki & Izsak 2004; Szolnoki & Szabo 2004.
review:051.difference:
